## One cooling law.
Two stable phases. — Equal depths recover the static-front condition. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/ki-2002/
Coverage: reading

θ_xx = Q = ∂V/∂θ
(θ_x)² / 2 = V(θ,P) − Vcold
Vwarm − Vcold = ∫[Tcold → Twarm] κ(T) Q(T,P) dT
Zero conductive flux at both endpoints therefore requires equal well depths. This is exactly the existing ZP saturation condition. The independent potential calculation recovers the same pressure and all three thermal-equilibrium intersections. Their temperatures, densities and depths at each pressure are retained in the JSON report.
Verification checks the derivative in θ, the curvature and local extrema of every equilibrium, independent composite Simpson quadrature, refinement from 16,001 to 32,001 quadrature points, the existing ZP integral and the sign of the depth difference. See the Ginzburg–Landau discussion for the static analogy. No compressible front speed or full time-dependent gas evolution is inferred from these curves.

## Reconstruct the mode.
Keep its components coupled. — Reconstruct the mode.
Keep its components coupled. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/kim-kim-2013/
Coverage: reading

Matching a growth-rate curve is only part of the task. The required result is the spatial eigenfunction, with its temperature, velocity, flux and pressure information preserved under one amplitude and phase convention.
This page defines the reconstruction and its acceptance criteria. No Kim2013 background front, eigenvalue, eigenfunction or source digitization has been computed in this project yet. Issue6 tracks the implementation. The original study is Kim & Kim, Instability of Evaporation Fronts in the Interstellar Medium.

## Reconstruct the mode.
Keep its components coupled. — Figure9 is the primary comparison. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/kim-kim-2013/
Coverage: reading

The MU69 example compares temperature and transverse velocity on two different transverse cuts. The reconstruction must produce both curves from the same mode:
Temperature panel: δT/Tbackground at y = 0.5Ly.
Velocity panel: δvy/vx1 at y = 0.25Ly.
Source comparison time: t/tgr = 2; pressure P/kB = 1800 K cm⁻³.
Table3 uses Ly = 1.06 pc; Table1 quotes the fastest wavelength as 1.05 pc. Keep that rounding distinction when selecting k.
Compare signs, extrema, zero crossings, relative amplitudes and far-field decay. Digitization must distinguish the source’s analytical solid curves from its simulation dots, and retain axis calibration and reading uncertainty. A common amplitude alignment can test shape and relative amplitude; matching the absolute amplitude after the source’s initially shifted front requires a separate initial-mode projection or linear initial-value calculation.
The origin is fixed by T = √(T1T2). Temperature divided by Tbackground is a pointwise conversion from the solver’s δT/T1, rather than the same plotted variable.

## Reconstruct the mode.
Keep its components coupled. — Match the paper’s background model first. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/kim-kim-2013/
Coverage: reading

The source uses the corrected KI cooling fit but a constant conductivity κ = 10⁵ erg cm⁻¹ s⁻¹ K⁻¹, with m = 1.37mH, n = ρ/m and γ = 5/3. Its reported saturation pressure is Psat/kB = 2282 K cm⁻³. The existing KI/Iwasaki benchmark instead uses κ = 2500√T and has a different computed saturation pressure. Copying its front unchanged would change the problem.
Reconstruct the steady boundary-value problem and its mass-flux eigenvalue from equations (9)–(13), before assembling the linear operator. Figures2–3 and Table1 provide background comparisons. Report residuals against the rounded source values; do not fit coefficients or redefine the origin to force agreement.

## Reconstruct the mode.
Keep its components coupled. — Five state components, one eigenfunction. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/kim-kim-2013/
Coverage: reading

xi = x / ell_D1
nu = k ell_D1
sigma = Omega / (k vx1)
state = (J, V, M, Theta, dTheta/dxi)
Theta = temperature Fourier amplitude / T1
AppendixA equations (A7)–(A10) form a five-dimensional first-order problem. The source’s state-vector order differs from the presentation order in (A6); it must be explicit in code. The upstream regular basis contains incompressible and thermal modes. Downstream it contains incompressible, vortex and thermal modes. Match the full state, using the regularity and outgoing-mode conditions of (A11)–(A21).
delta vy / vx1 = Re[ -i V(xi) exp(Omega t + i k y) ]
delta T / Tbackground
 = (T1/Tbackground) Re[ Theta(xi) exp(Omega t + i k y) ]
The growing branch may use real state amplitudes; the transverse-velocity Fourier amplitude still carries the explicit −i factor. This gives the transverse phase relation used by the two Figure9 cuts. Independent component normalizations or phase rotations would destroy that information.
Use the paper’s C1 = 1 convention, or a documented equivalent single gauge. Export all five state components, the basis coefficients and reconstructed physical perturbations, with units and the retained approximation order. The source’s low-Mach/isobaric reduction retains hydrodynamic coupling; it must not be replaced by setting pressure and velocity perturbations to zero or advertised as an exact full-compressible spectrum.

## Reconstruct the mode.
Keep its components coupled. — Required verification gates. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/kim-kim-2013/
Coverage: reading

Background: converge the thermal front, mass flux and energy balance before solving for perturbations.
Operator: independently check the linearization and heat-loss derivative, and substitute every far-field basis vector into the constant-state equations.
Eigenfunction: retain equation, matching and boundary residuals for all components. Use scale-aware norms without ratios through zero components.
Convergence: enlarge both far fields, refine the spatial representation and tighten tolerances. Both the eigenvalue and the normalized mode shape must converge.
Mode identity: follow the same branch by eigenfunction overlap as k changes. Recover the k = 0 translation mode and long-wave displacement limit without imposing them on finite-k modes.
Source comparison: reconstruct both Figure9 cuts with a common normalization. Validate a representative mode with an independent discretization or small-amplitude linear evolution.
Dispersion: then reproduce Figure5 at P/kB = 1700, 1800 and 1900 K cm⁻³. Its ordinate is ΩellD1/vx1 = νσ, not σ alone. Check (A24), the peak and the cutoff; the downstream vortex tail becomes long as σ approaches zero.
A full nonlinear two-dimensional run is a separate, optional task. The coupled Fourier-mode eigenproblem is the required core.

## Reconstruct the mode.
Keep its components coupled. — Source questions remain visible. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/kim-kim-2013/
Coverage: reading

The inspected v2 text on page5 gives Lf = 0.13 pc for the 1800 K cm⁻³ evaporation example, whereas Table1 gives 0.29 pc. This must be checked against the journal version and definitions. It is not a reason to tune a coordinate scale. The Figure9 initial-value amplitude convention also needs clarification before claiming an absolute-amplitude reproduction.

Source review: Original scan pp.108–109, Eq.2.14, Eqs3.2–3.6 and Figure1 visually checked. The paper allows general bistable cooling; the earlier Elphick–Regev–Spiegel1991 model used a cubic approximation.

## Track the scientific question.
Keep the limits visible. — Track the scientific question.
Keep the limits visible. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/progress.html
Coverage: reading

Each work item has a purpose, a completion condition, evidence and a published outcome. An unresolved diagnostic can be useful progress when its assumptions and restart conditions are recorded.
GitHub Issues are the live task record. This page is a dated guide to the current priorities and published work; consult the linked issues for later status changes. We normally keep one scientific implementation active at a time.

## Track the scientific question.
Keep the limits visible. — Latest result: pressure-dependent potential wells. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/progress.html
Coverage: reading

The KI2002 static-front potential comparison is implemented, numerically checked and published. It compares 0.9, 1 and 1.1 Psat with a shared normalization: the warm minimum is deeper below saturation, the wells have equal depth at saturation, and the cold minimum is deeper above saturation.
Code, configuration, curve CSV, equilibrium/depth records and desktop/mobile figures accompany the result. Independent quadrature, mesh refinement, derivatives and equilibrium curvatures verify the static correspondence to the ZP condition. No compressible front speed is inferred. Issue1 records the completed scope.

## Track the scientific question.
Keep the limits visible. — Queued next [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/progress.html
Coverage: reading

Kim & Kim2013: reconstruct the coupled Figure9 eigenfunctions. The source-audited specification makes component shapes, relative amplitudes, phase and boundary/domain convergence mandatory. This is the next major linear-analysis target now that the KI potential task is complete; no Kim solver has been implemented yet.
Explain pressure-driven compressible flow versus reduced reaction–diffusion models. Retain pressure, momentum, advection and compressional work, while distinguishing nearly uniform pressure from zero flow. Include Chandrasekhar’s Boussinesq convection as an intermediate fluid approximation, with buoyancy as a distinct driver.
Isolate one missing Iwasaki2012 branch or critical-flux example. A bounded trajectory diagnostic comes before another full-grid calculation.
Quantify Schwarz1972 condensation timing and mesh sensitivity. Reuse existing runs and retain source-reading, model and numerical uncertainties.

## Track the scientific question.
Keep the limits visible. — What the archive currently provides. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/progress.html
Coverage: reading

Historical simulation gallery: four 2D and four 3D full-frame recordings, an 18-second edited 3D introduction, and two source-traceable still illustrations. Materials MD is excluded. Complete media decode, source/output frame counts and provenance are checked; exact run inputs and paper-figure matches remain unverified. This is archival footage, not a newly validated simulation.
2D thermal-condensation cover: actual compressible evolution, movie, poster, initial/final states and independent numerical benchmarks. Deliberately enhanced conduction broadens interfaces; this is an illustrative model, not a historical reproduction or sustained turbulence.
Field1965 Figures1–3: calculations from the source equations, with numerical checks; pointwise digitized comparisons remain separate work.
KI2002 equilibrium benchmark: corrected coefficients, stability branches, planar ZP saturation and pressure-dependent potential wells with all equilibrium intersections.
Schwarz1972 linear calculation and nonlinear Lagrangian prototype: cooling, conduction and recombination with explicit historical-input and resolution limits.
Iwasaki2012 front-classification prototype: nine source examples agree; the published maps are not fully reproduced.
FGH/GHF equilibrium prototype: original-curve residuals and a conditional saturation search, with historical coefficient recovery deferred.

## From two phases
to chemistry and cloud formation. — From two phases
to chemistry and cloud formation. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/research-paths.html
Coverage: reading

FGH established a two-phase picture. Later work changed the heating and chemical inputs, then followed fronts, turbulence, and magnetized clouds. This reading list connects those questions to the calculations we can document and explore.
Listed references are not completed reproductions. Bibliography and abstracts have been checked; equations, target figures, and data availability need individual review. This page groups papers by research path; each path runs from oldest to newest. For one chronological list across all paths, open all papers by year. Publication years are used where confirmed, with preprint dates noted separately.

## From two phases
to chemistry and cloud formation. — Choose the scientific question before the computing budget. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/research-paths.html
Coverage: reading

Reproducing a large multidimensional simulation can require substantial computing time, storage, and access to original inputs. Our modern-paper exhibits can instead provide a source guide, documented setup, analysis of available outputs, or a small benchmark that isolates a physical mechanism.
Source and method: link the paper and any public code, inputs, and datasets; record what is actually available.
Reuse and analysis: regenerate a diagnostic from released outputs where possible, preserving units, provenance, and processing steps.
Small calculations: evaluate an analytic relation, a one-zone chemical model, a front, or a convergence test within an explicit reduced scope.
Optional full runs: record the resolution, solver, hardware, wall time, and storage needed. A full 2D/3D rerun is not a condition for completing a source or analysis exhibit.
For new nonlinear thermal-instability simulation exhibits, the thermal-conduction treatment and resolution of its relevant scales are selection criteria to audit explicitly. Analytical theory and microphysical rate references are documented separately. Digitized published curves will be identified as digitizations. Reduced models will state their omissions; their results will not be labeled as full-simulation reproductions.

to chemistry and cloud formation. — Foundations: thermal stability, buoyancy and conductive phase exchange [en]

Parker (1953) provides a pre-Field historical starting point. Chandrasekhar (1961) supplies the buoyancy-driven convection and Boussinesq comparison. Balbus (1986) extends the local stability analysis to evolving backgrounds, while Begelman & McKee (1990) treats conductive mass exchange between phases. Analytical background references and conduction-resolved simulation exhibits have different roles.

## From two phases
to chemistry and cloud formation. — Global Effects of Thermal Conduction on Two-Phase Media [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/research-paths.html
Coverage: reading

Convection and radiative condensation are distinct: Chandrasekhar’s textbook is included as a foundational monograph, not a journal paper. Its proposed benchmark is buoyancy-driven convection of a layer heated from below. Rayleigh-number onset must not be identified with the cooling-derivative criterion for the Field condensation mode, which does not require gravity.
The Boussinesq comparison retains velocity, a pressure constraint and buoyancy while filtering acoustic compressibility. It does not mean zero flow or zero pressure gradient. The resulting hierarchy for the proposed explanation is: selected reaction–diffusion models → Boussinesq fluid dynamics → compressible thermal gas. These are different approximations and drivers, not a single universal equation.
Spiegel & Veronis (1960), On the Boussinesq Approximation for a Compressible Fluid, gives a primary-source account of its assumptions: a thin layer relative to scale heights and suitably small fluctuations. Density variations remain in the buoyancy force. The compressible-fluid reduction also requires care with the adiabatic temperature gradient.
The textbook’s bibliography is checked; its exact equations, sections and figures are not yet audited because full-text access attempts failed. No textbook figure is claimed reproduced. Source review and proposed scope / JSON.

## From two phases
to chemistry and cloud formation. — Magnetic Flux Loss from Interstellar Clouds with Various Grain-Size Distributions [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/research-paths.html
Coverage: reading

Field et al. (1968) discusses Takayanagi and Nishimura’s H₂ excitation data. FGH (1969) cites Hayakawa, Nishimura and Takayanagi’s cosmic-ray heating work. Hattori, Nakano and Hayashi’s reference list includes both papers. These links identify a route for source tracing; they do not establish that later models use identical coefficients.
For each future rate record, we will distinguish cross sections, rate coefficients, energy-loss coefficients, volumetric rates, and yields. Species, colliders, units, normalization, validity range, population assumptions, source equation/table, and correction/code version will accompany the numerical formula.
The Takayanagi–Nishimura rate audit now transcribes 34 coefficients and tests a finite level model. Its Table 2 mismatches remain visible. Other coefficient sets still require equation/table review; the citation links alone do not validate them. Lineage evidence and proposed coefficient-record fields / JSON

## From two phases
to chemistry and cloud formation. — Magnetic Flux Loss from Interstellar Clouds with Various Grain-Size Distributions [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/research-paths.html
Coverage: reading

Ionization fraction is a separate branch: Nishi, Nakano & Umebayashi (1991) calculates electron, ion and charged-grain abundances before magnetic coupling. Figures1–4 compare grain distributions. Figure1 is a possible small charge-equilibrium benchmark, not a thermal-balance calculation. Its axes use abundances relative to total hydrogen nuclei and nH/ζ, with ζ the ionization rate per hydrogen molecule; these conventions must not be silently interchanged with FGH’s atomic-gas definitions.
The paper calls Umebayashi & Nakano (1990), Magnetic flux loss from interstellar clouds, MNRAS243,103–113, PaperI and builds on its reaction scheme. The publisher’s abstract confirms an ionization–recombination equilibrium calculation; its full rate-table audit remains pending. Distinguish the ionization rate ζ from the resulting electron fraction, and distinguish both from a cooling coefficient. Source review and parameter conventions / JSON.

## From two phases
to chemistry and cloud formation. — Instability of Evaporation Fronts in the Interstellar Medium [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/research-paths.html
Coverage: reading

Steady flow and perturbations: Ferrara & Shchekinov (1993) studies static/steady front properties and their dynamical evolution. Shchekinov & Ibáñez (2001) studies planar acoustic/entropy perturbations interacting with steady subsonic fronts. In section 3, Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) explicitly describes the latter work as determining the ZP mass flux j(P) through an eigenvalue problem. We will audit the steady background before attempting perturbation coefficients. This citation does not establish identical cooling laws or numerical parameters.
Related entries: Inoue, Inutsuka & Koyama (2006) addresses front stability; Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2012) studies dynamical condensation fronts; Iwasaki & Inutsuka (2014) studies interfacial energy transfer in a bistable medium. The Field-condition paper provides a connection to conduction and resolution.
Different heat-loss laws, geometries, and dynamical approximations must be preserved when comparing these studies. A reading path is not proof of identical assumptions or coefficients.

## From two phases
to chemistry and cloud formation. — Connect these references to the current exhibits. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/research-paths.html
Coverage: reading

The corrected KI2002 equilibrium benchmark includes stability branches, ZP saturation pressure and all three thermal-equilibrium intersections. Model-specific landmarks retain density conventions and unresolved cases. The Maxwell equal-area historical aside traces the primary publications and distinguishes its integral from ZP selection. The same aside develops a scalar Ginzburg–Landau connection, with Elphick, Regev & Shaviv (1992) as a direct precedent.
Field’s stability map connects to front and perturbation problems. FGH/GHF two-phase equilibrium prototype, historical ingredients, and reduced cold branch give a starting point for comparing historical and later microphysics.

## Let the background cool.
Watch the perturbations grow. — Let the background cool.
Watch the perturbations grow. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/schwarz-1972/
Coverage: reading

Cloud formation can begin while the surrounding gas cools, rather than departing from steady thermal equilibrium. Here the background temperature and ionization evolve together with density perturbations at four wavelengths.
First target: the early-time part of Figure 2. The linear equations include conduction and recombination. Cooling is reconstructed from Figure 1, rather than independently recovered from every atomic rate. The run stops at the input-data boundary, about 1.68 Myr. Late-time Figure 2 remains unfinished. A separate nonlinear Lagrangian prototype now follows the 3 pc, 10% perturbation into condensation.

## Let the background cool.
Watch the perturbations grow. — A time-dependent background changes the instability problem. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/schwarz-1972/
Coverage: reading

Solid lines: the declared linear prototype. Dashed black: background temperature, read on the right axis. Open circles: Figure 2 density readings; black crosses: its temperature readings. Gray: beyond the input domain. The right panel shows the reconstructed cooling input. There is no fitted time rescaling.SVGPNGBackground & perturbations / CSVFigure 2 comparison / CSVNumerical report / JSON
Initial conditions: n(H) =0.3 cm⁻³, T =8,200 K, x =n(e)/n(H) =0.05; neutral He/H =0.1. Wavelengths are 0.3,1,3,10 pc. The historical conduction prescription is K(T) =2,500√T in cgs units. No continuing heating is applied.
The 0.3 pc mode initially decreases, showing short-wavelength conduction damping. Within the computed window it later reaches about 14.8 times its initial amplitude, while the 1 pc mode reaches about 107. The latter maximum occurs at the domain stop and is not an established peak. These are normalized linear amplitudes, not nonlinear cloud density contrasts.
The original curves are not matched exactly. The report gives separate log-RMS discrepancies and scored-point counts for temperature and each wavelength. Points past the domain stop have no model prediction. These descriptive differences are not numerical pass tolerances.

## Let the background cool.
Watch the perturbations grow. — Integrate the background and perturbations together. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/schwarz-1972/
Coverage: reading

Equations (16)–(18) evolve uniform cooling and recombination. Equations (19)–(24) evolve relative density, pressure, velocity divergence, and ionization perturbations; the equation of state supplies the temperature perturbation. The coefficients change with time, so a single constant exponential growth rate is insufficient.
d ln T₀/dt = −1/τC + (2−γ)[x₀/(1.1+x₀)]/τR
d ln x₀/dt = −1/τR
τC = (1.1+x₀)kT₀ / [n₀(γ−1)Λ]
τR = 1/[n₀x₀α⁽²⁾(T₀)]
The pressure perturbation contains the conduction term in equation (19). Density amplitudes are normalized to n₁(0) =1; the actual perturbation may be arbitrarily small. Pressure, velocity and relative ionization perturbations initially vanish. This declared initial-mode choice has not been confirmed as the unique Figure 2 initialization.
DOP 853 and Radau agree on the computed evolution. Equation (19) is also compared with a centered-difference Jacobian of the original primitive pressure equation, including the changing background normalization.

## Let the background cool.
Watch the perturbations grow. — Keep the historical input limits visible. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/schwarz-1972/
Coverage: reading

The 39 Figure 1 readings cover x =0.001,0.01,0.1 and T ≈13.93–8,429.74 K. PCHIP interpolates logΛ(logT), with Λ piecewise linear in ionization fraction. A logarithmic-ionization alternative changes the stopping time to about 1.51 Myr, illustrating reconstruction sensitivity.
The accepted solution stops at the lowest supported temperature,13.93 K, after 1.679 Myr. It is not continued through an invented cold cooling law. Raw pixels, crop origins, calibration ticks and source hashes accompany the input. Figure 2 readings use the 0–2 Myr ticks bracketing the sampled interval; a single exact affine scale is not assumed for the slightly distorted full scan. Reading envelopes are practical limits, not statistical confidence intervals, and there is no independent second digitization.
H recombination uses Hjellming’s (1966) excited-state approximation; the exact fit used by Schwarz and collaborators remains unidentified. Nonpositive linear amplitudes remain in the CSV but are omitted from the log plot; they do not mean negative physical gas density.
This paper adopts Fe/H =5 ×10⁻⁵, compared with 8 ×10⁻⁶ in the earlier FGH baseline. Neither FGH nor KI cooling is silently substituted. Jura & Dalgarno’s Table 1 supplies several electron-impact rates but does not alone specify all required neutral channels.

into a cold, dense layer. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/schwarz-1972/nonlinear.html

A 10% density wave grows beyond the linear regime in a cooling 3 pc box. Moving mass cells follow the compression, while thermal conduction, recombination and shock heating act together.
A nonlinear numerical prototype, using 96 mass cells for the displayed profiles. There is no Riemann solver. The method uses pressure forces, compatible pressure work and compression-only artificial viscosity. Figures 3–6 motivate the outputs; original cooling inputs, timing and front resolution remain imperfect, so this is not certified historical reproduction.

## Follow the gas
into a cold, dense layer. — Density, velocity, temperature and ionization. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/schwarz-1972/nonlinear.html
Coverage: reading

Times are the same as the published snapshots; no temporal or phase shift was fitted. The displayed run uses 96 equal-H-mass cells. Both the mass coordinate and physical positions/cell widths are exported. The original figure labels zone number; its exact grid-to-mass mapping has not been recovered.Profiles / SVGPNGFull profiles / CSVMesh histories / CSVValidation & source comparison / JSON
At 0.985 Myr the displayed model has peak n(H) ≈ 31.1 cm⁻³, a density contrast ≈ 187, minimum temperature ≈ 12.7 K and minimum ionization fraction ≈ 0.0010. The surrounding warm minimum-density gas is about 1430 K. These are computed quantities, not prescribed cloud conditions.
The paper’s text gives approximate cloud values of 15 K, x ≈ 0.002, a 0.007 pc extent and 20% of the mass, with an intercloud temperature about 1,800 K. Our density-excess FWHM is 0.0078 pc, while the broader selection T < 100 K and n > 10 times the mean gives 0.0155 pc and 28.1% of the mass. These definitions need not coincide with the original cloud edge.
The condensation timing differs: by 0.955 Myr this prototype already has a strongly condensed layer, whereas the corresponding original profile is still growing. The resemblance of the late cloud does not establish pointwise agreement throughout the evolution.

## Follow the gas
into a cold, dense layer. — A classical Lagrangian calculation. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/schwarz-1972/nonlinear.html
Coverage: reading

The periodic domain contains a sinusoidal physical-space density perturbation of amplitude 0.1 and wavelength 3 pc, with mean n(H) = 0.3 cm⁻³. The unperturbed temperature is 8,200 K, x = 0.05, and neutral He/H = 0.1. Initial pressure is uniform, so the local temperature varies inversely with density; velocities start at zero.
Equal-H-mass cells move with the gas. A compatible midpoint pressure-work update balances changes in internal and kinetic energy. Compression-only quadratic and linear artificial viscosity handle shocks. Conduction uses a conservative periodic implicit solve, and a coupled local energy/recombination solve accounts for radiative losses and changing particle number.
This is not the recovered original program. The paper describes von Neumann–Richtmyer viscosity and 100–200 spatial mesh points. The 64/96-cell cases explore historical-scale calculations below that reported range; the 128-cell case lies within it. We keep these experiments separate from any claim about the authors’ exact mesh.
The semi-implicit conduction update is backward Euler. We therefore do not claim global second-order time accuracy; timestep refinement is measured directly. No temperature floor, clipped density, imposed cold layer or fitted time shift is used.

## Follow the gas
into a cold, dense layer. — Compare mesh counts without declaring every front resolved. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/schwarz-1972/nonlinear.html
Coverage: reading

64, 96 and 128 cells are the historical-scale study; 512 cells provide an auxiliary comparison. The dashed temperature line is the input boundary. The four-cell Field-length line is a stated diagnostic, not a universal theorem, and is not met throughout these runs.Mesh comparison / SVGPNG
At 0.985 Myr the 96-to-128 density-profile L1 difference on mass coordinate is about 3.2%; 128 versus 512 differs by about 4.7%. Halving the timestep in the 96-cell calculation changes the density profile by about 0.02%. Profiles are compared without shifting the cloud.
Spatial front resolution is still limited. The auxiliary 512-cell run reaches a minimum Field-length proxy of only 1.37 cells. The proxy is √[K(T)T/(n²Λ)]. A small difference between these cloud profiles is not proof that the thin conductive interface or a continuum solution is fully resolved.
All 33 numerical self-checks pass, including compatible hydro energy accounting, a periodic conduction Fourier mode, independent cooling/recombination ODEs, the small-amplitude linear limit, box length, momentum, positivity and timestep agreement. The unmet spatial-resolution diagnostic is recorded separately and is not counted as a passed check.

## Follow the gas
into a cold, dense layer. — Track where the cooling input is extended. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/schwarz-1972/nonlinear.html
Coverage: reading

The nonlinear cooling table adds 12 warm-end readings to the earlier 39 points from Figure 1. These cover the locally warmer cells in the initially isobaric wave. The earlier linear input and results are preserved.
Below the lowest graph temperature, about 13.93 K, the model uses a continuous C II-like asymptote with exp(−92/T), neutral-collider T⁰ and electron-collider T⁻¹ᐟ² factors. Below x = 0.001 the two low-ionization curves continue to a nonnegative neutral-collider contribution. These are explicit extrapolations, not recovered historical coefficients.
The 96-cell density contrast first reaches 100 near 0.948 Myr. It enters the cold temperature extension near 0.974 Myr and the low-ionization extension near 0.986 Myr. Thus the initial formation of the high-contrast layer precedes those extensions, while the later cloud state depends on them. Exposure of each accepted state is recorded in the report.
Changing the cold electron temperature power from −1/2 to 0 is included as a sensitivity probe. It does not bound every uncertainty in the historical cooling rates. The recombination fit, normalization caveat and proof note described in the linear exhibit remain relevant.

## Follow a rate coefficient
into molecular cooling. — Follow a rate coefficient
into molecular cooling. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/takayanagi-nishimura-1960/
Coverage: reading

Before a cooling function becomes one line of code, it depends on collision partners, transition directions, level populations, and radiative losses. Here we trace those steps through a historical H₂ calculation.
Scope: 34 printed excitation coefficients and a declared finite-level calculation, compared with 60 printed cooling values. This is not a complete reproduction of the original cooling model. Numerical checks and differences from the source table are reported separately.

## Follow a rate coefficient
into molecular cooling. — From H-atom collisions to para-H₂ radiation. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/takayanagi-nishimura-1960/
Coverage: reading

Table 1, printed p. 82: thermally averaged upward excitation coefficients. The right panel uses those coefficients, equations (7) and (9), and the photon-energy definition on p. 83. Lines connect computed samples, while crosses show the source cooling values. No interpolated coefficients enter the calculation.SVGPNG34 rate records / CSVLevel populations & cooling / CSV
The coefficient qup has units cm³ s⁻¹. It counts excitations per collider–target pair; it is not yet an energy-loss coefficient. To obtain radiation, we must also determine the excited-state population and the energy carried by a decay.
These are the temperatures and channels printed in the 1960 source. The authors discuss limitations of their collision approximation and temperature-dependent accuracy; numerical reproduction of a coefficient does not establish that it is an accurate modern rate.

## Follow a rate coefficient
into molecular cooling. — Keep upward rates, downward rates, and energy losses distinct. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/takayanagi-nishimura-1960/
Coverage: reading

qdown = qup [(2J−3)/(2J+1)] exp[170.68(2J−1)/T]
pJ/pJ−2 = n(H)qup / [n(H)qdown + AJ→J−2]
L / n(para-H₂) = ΣJ pJAJ→J−2ΔEJ,J−2
J denotes the upper state of a pair of adjacent even rotational levels. The population fractions sum to one. n(H) is the H-atom collider density, rather than the total hydrogen-nuclei density. The final cooling is in erg s⁻¹ per para-H₂ molecule; multiplying by its number density gives erg cm⁻³ s⁻¹.
The historical spontaneous-emission formula is A = 7.52 × 10⁻¹³ J(J−1)(2J−1)⁴/(2J+1) s⁻¹. The photon energy is ΔE = 2.3561 × 10⁻¹⁴(2J−1) erg. Both are retained as printed, without substituting modern coefficients.

## Follow a rate coefficient
into molecular cooling. — What does a blank table entry mean? [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/takayanagi-nishimura-1960/
Coverage: reading

Table 1 provides fewer transitions at lower temperatures. Its missing entries are preserved as unavailable inputs. At each temperature this experiment closes the ladder at the highest connected level for which an upward coefficient is listed: J = 2, 4, 6, or 8.
That is an explicit truncation of the model. It does not establish a zero physical rate to higher levels. The calculation includes H-atom collisions, para-H₂, and optically thin spontaneous emission at fixed gas temperature. It does not include ortho-H₂, other colliders, line trapping, gas chemistry, or a gas thermal-equilibrium solution.

## Follow a rate coefficient
into molecular cooling. — Show the mismatch as part of the result. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/takayanagi-nishimura-1960/
Coverage: reading

100 × (finite-ladder calculation / printed cooling − 1), for 60 reference points. These are measured discrepancies, not passed validation tests. The source row that appears as 155 K in Table 2, while Table 1 gives 150 K, is excluded pending clarification.SVGPNGPrinted values & differences / CSV
The largest discrepancy is at T = 200 K and n(H) = 100 cm⁻³. The restricted calculation gives 4.6578 × 10⁻²⁵ erg s⁻¹ per molecule, compared with 5.95 × 10⁻²⁵ in the printed table: a difference of approximately −21.72%.
We have not established the cause. Additional level/rate information or a source correction may be needed before assigning an explanation. The input coefficients are left unchanged, and the discrepancy remains in the downloadable comparison.

## Watch an unstable medium
form cold clouds. — Equations and deliberate choices. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/ti-2d/
Coverage: reading

Periodic 4.8 × 3.0 pc box, 256 × 160 cells (Δx = Δy = 0.01875 pc). The compressible Euler equations include momentum, advection, compressional work, thermal conduction and net radiative cooling. There is no forcing, magnetic field, gravity or evolving chemistry.
γ = 5/3; m = 1.37 mH; n = ρ/m; P = nkBT. Mean density is 2.8 cm⁻³, initially at unstable thermal equilibrium. A seeded low-wave-number density perturbation has 10% RMS; temperature adjusts to keep initial pressure uniform and velocity starts at zero.
Γ = 2 × 10⁻²⁶ erg s⁻¹ per particle; Q = n²Λ(T) − nΓ. We use the corrected KI-type analytic cooling fit, evaluating its density argument as the explicitly defined n above. This is a phenomenological model with no separate ionization solution.
κ(T) = 3 × 10⁶ + 3 × 10⁸(100 K / T)² erg cm⁻¹ s⁻¹ K⁻¹. This enlarged, cold-enhanced coefficient broadens thermal interfaces for a modest grid. It differs from the Parker law and the conductivity in the KI equilibrium benchmark. Its own ZP saturation pressure and equilibrium intersections are recorded in diagnostics.json; those values must not replace the existing KI/Parker result.

## Watch an unstable medium
form cold clouds. — Equations and deliberate choices. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/ti-2d/
Coverage: reading

The finite-volume solver uses MC-limited reconstruction, HLLC fluxes, SSPRK2, harmonic-face conductive fluxes, and explicit radiative sources. Time steps respect hyperbolic, diffusion and cooling constraints. Invalid stages cause a smaller step; there are no density or temperature floors, clipping, mass sinks or imposed condensations. The source lookup covers 2–30000 K without extrapolation.

## Watch an unstable medium
form cold clouds. — Check the flow before trusting the picture. [en]

Source: https://koyamahr.github.io/the-art-of-thermal-instability/ti-2d/
Coverage: reading

The numerical report tests an analytically advected contact, continuum heat-equation decay, isochoric cooling against independent adaptive integration, and a compressible linear TI eigenmode derived from a separate Fourier-space matrix. Density, velocity and pressure are checked together. The movie run also has mass and radiative-energy accounting checks.
At 12 Myr, the cold mass fraction (T < 300 K) is 80.77%, compared with 80.93% on 128 × 80 cells. Mean P/kB is 1732.99 versus 1732.09 K cm⁻³. Maximum sampled Mach number is 0.380; the movie shows subsonic condensation.
Relative mass drift is 1.55e-14; relative radiative-energy ledger residual is 1.36e-13. No positivity retries or HLLE fallbacks occurred. Minimum sampled Field proxy is 3.98 cells on the main grid: approximately four, with a small interval below four, so a strict four-cell target is not met everywhere. The movie is an illustrative result, not a resolved-interface convergence benchmark.
The Field proxy √[κT/(n²Λ)] is an energy-balance estimate, not the exact marginal wavelength or measured interface width. Values above are sampled at history output times, not at every RK stage. A few cells in this proxy and agreement of global quantities do not establish continuum convergence of cloud morphology. The coarse grid is a sensitivity comparison, not a second physical model.
